faq.q: Will the ₹ rupee sign and Hindi text print correctly in the PDF?
faq.a: Yes. Instead of embedding a limited PDF font that only covers Latin letters, each sheet is drawn onto a high-resolution canvas using the fonts your browser already has, and that canvas is embedded into the PDF. So any Unicode text the browser can display — the ₹ symbol, Devanagari, Tamil, Marathi — prints exactly as it looks, rather than turning into boxes or question marks.

faq.q: My sheet has 25 columns and they run off the page. What can I do?
faq.a: Two options under 'When columns don't fit'. 'Fit to width' scales every column down proportionally so they all sit across one page (combine with landscape for very wide sheets). 'Split columns across pages' keeps the font size and continues the extra columns on following pages, repeating the first column as a label so you can still tell which row is which.

faq.q: Does it keep merged title cells, column widths and show numbers the way Excel does?
faq.a: Yes. Merged ranges from the workbook's !merges are drawn as a single spanning cell, column widths from !cols (wpx or wch) and row heights from !rows are honoured when present, numeric cells are right-aligned by default, and the header row can be bolded. Crucially it uses each cell's formatted text (SheetJS .w), so a date, percentage or currency value reads the same as it does in Excel rather than as a raw number.

faq.q: Can I convert only some sheets, and how is the file named?
faq.a: Every sheet in the workbook is listed with a checkbox, so you convert exactly the ones you tick and each starts fresh in the combined PDF. If you convert a single sheet the file is saved as <file>-<sheet>.pdf; if you convert several it is saved as <file>.pdf. Empty sheets are skipped and reported.
